units.title: Classification of Drugs in Part 2
units.sec: Classification of Drugs in Part 2 · p118
units.guide: Part 2 continues the classification with K+ channel openers (ezogabine/retigabine, whose production stopped in 2017 and which causes blue pigmentation of lips/nails and retinal deposits), drugs decreasing glutamate effect - AMPA blockers perampanel and telampanel, and the NMDA blocker felbamate (for GTCS/PS, no longer used, causing bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity) - drugs increasing GABA effect (GABAA channel openers, reuptake inhibitors, GABA transaminase inhibitors and GABA analogues) and miscellaneous drugs such as cannabidiol (for LGS and DS, with hepatotoxicity limiting use below 2 years) and the SV2A modulator group (levetiracetam and brivaracetam, used in GTCS, m.s. and status epilepticus). These are common in PS and are used as add-on drugs.

units.title: GABA-related Drugs and Miscellaneous Agents
units.sec: GABA-related Drugs and Miscellaneous Agents · p119
units.guide: The GABA synapse sketch shows glutamate driving GABA formation with calcium entry; GABA analogues pregabalin and gabapentin act on the alpha-2-delta subunit of the Ca2+ channel and are used in peripheral neuropathy, post herpetic neuralgia, persistent leg movement (restless leg syndrome) and pain of spinal cord injury; they are excreted unchanged so there are no drug interactions and cause daytime somnolence. Tiagabine blocks GABA reuptake, while vigabatrin blocks GABA transaminase and is used in infantile spasm with tuberous sclerosis (without tuberous sclerosis ACTH is used) but causes visual field defects. GABAA chloride channels in the brain are opened by ganoxolone (infantile spasm), benzodiazepines, barbiturates and stiripentol (Dravet syndrome), whereas baclofen acts on GABAB Gi in the spinal cord and is used in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; the shared actions are antiepileptic, sedation, anxiolysis and muscle relaxation. In JME not responding to first and second line drugs, polytherapy is used.
